analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to all wages above $250,000, ending the tax cap for high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by two House members, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, wages above a yearly cap (about $118,500 in 2016) are exempt from the Social Security payroll tax, so the highest earners stop paying into the system partway through the year. This bill would tax every dollar of wages and self-employment income above $250,000, and cover the gap between the cap and $250,000 as well — in effect removing the exemption for high earners. The extra revenue would shore up Social Security's finances; benefits themselves would not change.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries and future retirees, because the program's trust fund would receive more revenue and its solvency gap would shrink. Middle- and middle-high earners also gain relatively, since the tax burden would no longer stop at the cap while their own taxes continue on every dollar.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: The bill applies the Social Security payroll tax to wages and self-employment income above $250,000, and covers income between the annual cap and $250,000, so high earners would pay the tax on all of their earnings instead of stopping partway through the year [S2][S3].
The change would take effect for pay after December 31, 2016, sending additional revenue into the Social Security system, which is funded almost entirely by this payroll tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and the self-employed making over $250,000, who would pay the 12.4% combined payroll tax on income that is currently exempt above the cap. Employers would pay the matching half on those wages.

drawbacks.text: High earners would pay billions more in payroll tax without any corresponding increase in their own Social Security benefits, since the bill changes the tax side only; critics view that as breaking the historical link between what people pay in and what they get out [S3].

Self-employed professionals and owners of successful businesses would bear the full 12.4% tax on income above $250,000 themselves, a substantial new cost for small-business owners in high-income fields [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost falls entirely on the top slice of earners and their employers, while the benefit — a longer-lasting Social Security trust fund — is broadly shared. The main honest objection is that taxing high earners without crediting their extra taxes toward benefits changes Social Security's insurance-like character into something more redistributive. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much one values the program's solvency versus the traditional contribution-benefit link.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on July 14, 2016, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over payroll taxes [S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the wage cap keep paying no Social Security tax on income above roughly $118,500, and the solvency question the bill targeted remains unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the wage cap

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend Social Security payroll taxes to income above $250,000.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: High-income households and the self-employed earning over $250,000
industries.note: They would pay the 12.4% Social Security tax on income now exempt above the cap. Their interest in keeping the cap runs against the program's solvency, which benefits the broader public.
Employers pay the matching half of the payroll tax, so firms with highly paid staff would owe more. Their savings from the cap come at the trust fund's expense.

industries.industry: Social Security beneficiaries and the retirement system
industries.note: Additional payroll tax revenue would extend the trust fund's life, protecting benefits that tens of millions of retirees and disabled workers rely on.
